rationale: A wins because it finds four real, structurally different stories and tells the founder which ones are loaded guns before they pitch. Its pricing angle, "Nobody has settled on what an AI agent should cost, including Airtable," uses one of the update's most uncomfortable facts instead of walking past it. B's sharpest line, "won't say how often they get it right," is useful but overplays nondisclosure into an accusation and leaves the pricing story on the floor.
gaps_in_A: "bets the company on agents" overstates the facts. The update says Airtable is repositioning and launching agents, not making an existential bet.
"an established category leader" and the Notion/Smartsheet/Monday comparison add outside category claims. Plausible, but not supplied in the update.
"an $11B mark set in a different market" is an inference that needs sourcing. The update only says $11B, down from a higher peak.
The decay labels are confident despite A admitting "no prior coverage links were provided." Treat those as editorial assumptions, not facts.
gaps_in_B: "won't say how often they get it right" turns "agent-reliability data is not disclosed" into a refusal. That only works if Airtable was asked and declined, which is not in evidence.
"The prevailing belief is that 2025-26's selling point for enterprise AI is autonomy" is an invented trend claim unless backed with outside reporting.
"late to a crowded category" and "a company that needs one" are speculative color. Mean, maybe true, but not grounded in the fact block.
B misses the pricing angle entirely, even though "pricing for the agent features not finalized" is one of the cleanest reporter hooks in the update.
